frontmatter_description: Diagnose when the core issue is shaping the impression other people form of THE SPEAKER, through self-description, disclosure order, framing, or image management.
title: Self-Presentation and Impression Management
use_when: Use when the central question is what impression the actor wants OTHERS to form of THEM (competent, likable, modest, credible).
Use when the key lever is how the actor shapes self-information: what to reveal first, what to emphasize or omit, how to describe themselves.
Use when the actor manages their own overall image or identity for an audience (bio, introduction, interview, first impression, profile).
Use when the same true facts told in a different order or framing would change how the actor is seen.
do_not_use_when: Do not use when the actor is hiding or softening one FEELING to be polite, fit a role, or protect another person's feelings (the gift is ugly but they say 'I love it'); that is emotion display rules, even if an image-flavored answer is offered as a distractor.
Do not use when the question is only WHY a single utterance is phrased a certain way (politeness, saving face, probing) rather than what self-image is being built; that is speaking motive.
Do not use when the actor is one-way persuading someone about an EXTERNAL claim or request (go to the park, lend the laptop); that is persuasion, not self-presentation.
Do not use when the main issue is whether information should stay private at all; use privacy and boundaries instead.
Do not use when the main issue is apology or repairing harm after an offense; use relationship repair instead.
decision_variable: what impression of THE SPEAKER the speaker wants others to form, and how they shape self-information to get it
trigger_checklist: Is the target of management the SPEAKER'S OWN image, not another person's feelings and not an external proposal?
Is the lever the shaping of self-information: order of disclosure, emphasis, omission, or self-description?
Could the same true facts, reordered or reframed, change how the speaker is seen?
Is the goal a desired identity (competent, modest, likable, credible), not the concealment of a single emotion?
Is the scope the broad self-picture, not one protected secret, one apology, or one persuasion target?
workflow: Identify WHO is being managed: the speaker's own image (this unit), another person's feelings (emotion display rules), or someone's decision about an external claim (persuasion).
If it is the speaker's own image, confirm the lever is shaping self-information: order, emphasis, omission, or self-description.
Name the desired impression the speaker is building (competent, modest, likable, credible).
Reject distractors that frame the motive as sparing another's feelings or as winning a request, unless the scene's pivot really is the speaker's self-image.

Watch the trap: a white-lie to protect SOMEONE ELSE is NOT self-presentation even when an answer option says 'to build a good image'; pick image only when the speaker's own standing is the actual driver.
Choose the option whose motive is the impression the speaker wants others to form of THEM.

special_case.title: Truthful facts, reordered for image vs. an image-flavored distractor on a kindness lie
special_case.rule: Two traps sit on opposite sides. (1) Truthful statements ARE self-presentation when the pivot is which facts to lead with, emphasize, or omit to signal an identity. (2) But when someone tells a kind lie to spare ANOTHER person's feelings, an answer option that says 'to build her own good image' is a DISTRACTOR, not the gold; the driver is the other person's feelings.

worked_example.scene: Aunt Wang dislikes Uncle Zhang's dish but tells him it is the most delicious she has ever eaten; one answer says she does it to build her own good image in the community.
worked_example.question: Is this self-presentation, and why?
worked_example.answer_logic: No. The pivot is sparing Uncle Zhang's embarrassment, so it is emotion display rules / sparing feelings. The 'build her own image' option is a self-presentation distractor that is wrong, because her OWN standing is not what is actually driving the lie.

boundary_exit_rule: If the pivot is hiding or softening ONE feeling to be polite, fit a role, or spare another's feelings, exit to the skill for emotion display rules / sparing feelings; this is the most common trap.
If the pivot is only WHY a single utterance is phrased that way (politeness, saving face, probing), exit to the skill for speaking motive at the utterance level.
If the pivot is one-way persuasion of someone about an external claim or request, exit to the skill for persuasion.
If the core question becomes whether information should be shared at all, exit to the skill for privacy and boundaries.
If the core question becomes how to respond after an offense or damage, exit to the skill for repair and apology.

If the scene is a full first-impression or formal-interaction situation rather than a single self-presentation diagnostic, treat self-presentation as one component and apply the broader social-interaction capability.

references.route_signal: Route here when the scene's pivot is how the SPEAKER shapes their own self-information (order, emphasis, omission, self-description) to control the impression others form of THEM.
hard_boundary: Emotion display rules cover hiding or softening one FEELING to be polite or to protect another person; this unit covers managing the speaker's OVERALL self-image. A kind lie to spare someone is display rules even if an option says 'to build her own good image'.
Speaking motive asks why a single sentence is phrased a certain way; this unit asks what self-image the speaker is building across what they reveal.
Persuasion is one-way influence on someone's decision about an external claim; this unit is about the speaker's own projected identity, not winning a request.
Privacy asks whether information may be shared at all; this unit assumes presentation is happening and asks how it is shaped.
Repair fixes harm after a social break; this unit is about image before or apart from any offense.
shortcut_to_avoid: Do not equate impression management with lying; truthful ordering and framing can be self-presentation.
Do not pick this unit just because an answer option mentions 'image', 'reputation', or 'looking good'; if the real driver is sparing another's feelings, those are wrong distractors.
Do not collapse self-presentation into secrecy; the variable is the intended impression, not whether a fact is concealed.
common_failure_modes: Choosing self-image on a kind-lie scene because an option says 'to build a good image', when the real driver is protecting the other person's feelings.
Reading any selective disclosure as deception rather than truthful framing for image.
Confusing managing the speaker's OWN image with managing another person's emotion.
Missing that disclosure ORDER alone (what is led with) can be the diagnostic clue for self-presentation.

minimal_pair.case: A job candidate leads her self-introduction with team-leadership experience and saves the recent employment gap for later.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: She is ordering her own self-information to shape how competent she looks; the target managed is HER image, so this is self-presentation.

minimal_pair.case: Aunt Wang hates the dish but tells the cook it is delicious; one option says she does it to build her good image in the community.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: The driver is sparing the cook's feelings, not her own standing, so this is emotion display rules; the 'good image' option is a self-presentation distractor that is wrong.

boundary_stress_test: Swap who is protected: if the lie shields ANOTHER person's feelings it is display rules; if it builds the speaker's own standing it is self-presentation.
Reorder the same true facts: if the impression of the speaker changes, this unit applies; if nothing about self-image is at stake, it does not.
If the scene's goal is to get someone to agree to an external request, the center of gravity is persuasion, not self-presentation.
references.generalization_note: This unit covers bios, introductions, interviews, first impressions, profiles, selective disclosure, and ordering or framing of self-information whenever the primary variable is the impression others should form of the speaker.

validation_seed.positive_pattern: The speaker orders or frames their own self-information to look competent, modest, credible, or likable.
validation_seed.near_miss_pattern: The speaker tells a kind lie to spare another person's feelings, and an option falsely frames it as building the speaker's own image.
validation_seed.boundary_pattern: The speaker is persuading someone about an external request, or apologizing after harm, not managing their self-image.

notes: Keep the unit narrow: managing the SPEAKER'S OWN image only, not all communication strategy.
Primary trap: kind lies that protect another person are display rules, even when an 'image' option is dangled.
Diagnostic cue: 'Is the speaker shaping how others see HIM/HER, by choosing what to reveal first, emphasize, or omit?'
core_question: Manage self-information, image, disclosure order, and self-description
